code_findings: No code field; nothing to run. No sources; definitions are standard (background knowledge, not verified against a cited page).
reasons: Definitions correct. Two accuracy issues: the recession example is arguably concept drift (same profiles default more) so 'defaulters still look like past defaulters' is a stretch; and 'directly detect covariate drift' glosses that a P(X) change is also produced by label shift, so label-free monitoring detects input drift, not the type.

issues.claim: Example: a recession lifts the default rate from 3% to 6%, while defaulters still look like past defaulters.
issues.problem: Recessions usually also change P(y|X); example is only pure label drift under a strong assumption.
issues.replacement: Example: a recession lifts the default rate from 3% to 6%; this is pure label drift only if defaulters still look like past defaulters, which rarely holds exactly, so real cases are often a mix of label and concept drift.

issues.claim: you can directly detect covariate drift, by comparing feature distributions between a reference and a recent window (PSI, KS).
issues.problem: A P(X) shift cannot by itself show P(y|X) is unchanged, nor distinguish covariate from label shift (P(X) moves when P(y) moves).
issues.replacement: you can directly detect a change in the input distribution P(X), by comparing feature distributions between a reference and a recent window (PSI, KS); this flags input drift but cannot on its own show whether P(y|X) is unchanged or whether the cause is covariate or label shift.

reasons: Sessionisation query verified (exact 1800 s stays; 31 min splits; midnight crossing; duplicate timestamps) and the julianday claim is true: for 960 of 1440 exact-30-minute gaps julianday*86400 > 1800 (e.g. 1800.0000134).
One overstated claim about duplicate-timestamp ordering and a questionable 'be explicit' recommendation; in SQLite both windows sort identically so results are right, but this is not guaranteed.

issues.claim: duplicate timestamps give a zero gap, so their LAG order does not change the sessions.
issues.problem: Overstated. The tied rows' order inside LAG and inside the ROWS-frame SUM is not defined by ORDER BY event_ts; if the two windows ordered ties differently, the flagged tied row could land in the previous session. SQLite sorts identical windows the same way (my duplicate tests at session start were correct), but it is not guaranteed.
issues.replacement: duplicate timestamps give a zero gap, so they never start a session of their own; the order of tied rows is not defined by ORDER BY event_ts alone, so for a guaranteed-deterministic result add a unique tie-breaker such as rowid to both ORDER BY clauses.

issues.claim: the default RANGE frame would also work here but treats equal timestamps as peers, so be explicit.
issues.problem: The default RANGE frame is actually the order-insensitive choice for tied timestamps (all peers get the same running sum), so 'be explicit' with ROWS is only safe with a tie-breaker.
issues.replacement: the default RANGE frame would also work here and treats equal timestamps as peers (tied rows all get the same running sum); an explicit ROWS frame is the usual idiom but then needs a unique tie-breaker in the ORDER BY.

code_findings: No code field. Claims run on 3.13 and 3.10: PurePosixPath('a')/'/b' -> /b; PurePosixPath('a\\b').parts -> single part; b.tar.gz suffix .gz stem b.tar; .bashrc suffix ''; PureWindowsPath case-insensitive equal. All true.
reasons: Answer argues for pathlib correctly, but does not address the failure direction in the question (Linux-style paths failing on Windows) and ends with an overstated 'no functional gap' claim.

issues.claim: That is the usual reason Windows-style strings break on Linux.
issues.problem: The question describes the opposite direction (paths copied from Linux fail on a Windows machine). Windows accepts '/' as separator, so the typical causes are Linux absolute paths such as /home/u/data.csv (no drive letter; verified PureWindowsPath('/home/u/data.csv').is_absolute() is False), hard-coded separators in strings, and case/separator assumptions. pathlib does not fix hard-coded absolute Linux paths.
issues.replacement: That is the usual reason Windows-style strings break on Linux. In the opposite direction (Linux paths on Windows), '/' separators mostly work, so the failures come from absolute paths like /home/u/data.csv (no drive, so not absolute on Windows), hard-coded locations and case assumptions; pathlib does not fix those, so keep base directories in configuration and build everything below them with / .

issues.claim: there is no functional gap that forces you to keep it
issues.problem: Overstated: os.path.expandvars, os.path.relpath (Path.relative_to refuses '..' walks before 3.12; verified error on 3.10) and os.path.commonpath have no exact Path equivalents.
issues.replacement: os.path remains fine for quick string work, and a few helpers (expandvars, relpath with '..', commonpath) have no exact Path equivalent, but nothing forces you to keep it for new code.

issues.claim: 2. Import the module, not the name: import customers, then call customers.get_customer(...) inside functions.
issues.problem: Changing only one side is not enough. Verified: with both modules using from-imports, switching only orders to 'import customers' still fails for 'import orders'. issues.claim: The format is defined by PyPA specifications, but I did not open them in this task, so check the packaging guide for the exact field list.
issues.problem: First-person process note does not belong in a reference answer and leaves the pyproject part of the question under-answered. WebFetch of packaging.python.org was refused here, so I checked by parsing a sample with tomllib only (structure valid), not against the spec text.
issues.replacement: The format is defined by the PyPA pyproject.toml specification (see the 'Writing your pyproject.toml' guide). For the library, [project] holds name, version, requires-python, dependencies (abstract ranges), optional-dependencies (e.g. a 'dev' or 'test' extra) and [project.scripts] for entry points; for the service, keep the same table with loose requirements and a lock file beside it.
